pages.text: Empires of the World

image.note: Cover: four crowns/emblems ringing a world map

pages.text: Contents. What Makes an Empire? / Byzantium / The Ottomans / Ming China / The Aztecs / Why Empires Rise and Fall.

Say the word "empire" and most people picture Rome: its legions, its roads, its rulers in purple. Rome was mighty. But it was only one empire among many. Across the centuries, on three different continents, other empires rose that were just as vast, just as clever, and in some ways even grander.

This book visits four of them. Two you may never have heard of. One built a city on a lake. One sent ships the size of a football pitch across the ocean. Their stories are held together by two simple questions.

image.note: Four small vignettes framed together: a walled city, a domed capital, a floating city on a lake, and a fleet of great ships

pages.text: An empire is not just a large country. It is one ruler, and one government, stretching out over many different peoples: different lands, different languages, different gods, all bound under a single crown. That is what makes an empire different from a kingdom. It swallows others.

image.note: Simple diagram: one crown over many peoples

pages.text: You have met empires already. The gold of Ghana. The libraries of Mali. The armies of Songhai. The Oyo of the Yoruba, whose power spread across the forests of West Africa. Africa built great empires long before many others did.
So empires are old, and they are everywhere. But here is the strange thing. However far apart they stand, however different their people, almost every empire can be understood through two questions.

image.note: A world globe ringed by four small empire emblems, with two large question marks above it

pages.text: The first question is this: what held it together? What kept so many different peoples loyal to one distant ruler, year after year?

The answer is usually some mixture of the same things. A strong army. Good roads for soldiers and traders. Trusted coins and busy markets. A ruler people feared or admired. And often a shared belief that bound strangers together.

image.note: Four icons: army, road, coin, temple

pages.text: The second question is the harder one: what pulled it apart? Because every empire in this book, however mighty, came to an end.
Here too the answers rhyme. An empire grows too big to govern. Rivals circle. The money runs dry. A stronger enemy arrives. Or, strangest of all, an empire simply chooses to turn away from the world.

image.note: Four symbols of decline in a row: a toppling crown, an empty coffer, crossed swords at a border, a closed gate

pages.text: Keep those two questions in your mind. Carry them across oceans and centuries. We begin where Rome ended, with an empire that refused to die.

image.note: Turn-page arrow toward a domed city

chapters.title: Byzantium: the Rome That Would Not Die

pages.text: When Rome fell, it did not fall all at once. The western half crumbled. But the eastern half stood firm, and went on standing for another thousand years. Historians call it the Byzantine Empire. Its people had a simpler name for themselves. They called themselves Romans.

image.note: Map: western Rome faded, east glowing

pages.text: Their capital was Constantinople, one of the greatest cities the world has ever seen. It sat on a narrow strip of water between two continents, with Europe on one shore and Asia on the other. Every ship, every trader, every idea passing between them had to pass by its harbour.

image.note: Aerial of Constantinople on the strait

pages.text: This was the empire's first great strength: position. Whoever held Constantinople held the door between East and West, and could grow rich simply by guarding it.

image.note: Trade routes converging on the city

pages.text: At the city's heart stood Hagia Sophia, a church crowned by a dome so wide and so high that visitors said it seemed to hang from heaven on a golden chain. For almost a thousand years it was the largest building in the world. People wept when they walked inside.

image.note: Interior of Hagia Sophia, vast dome

pages.text: The emperor ruled from a glittering palace, seen as the head of both the empire and its church. His word was law. Around him spun a whole world of officials, generals, and clever advisers, each watching the others.

The empire's coins, the gold bezant, were trusted from Britain to China. A merchant in a far bazaar would take a bezant when he trusted nothing else. Good money, like a good army, holds an empire together.
And the city could defend itself. Its walls were the strongest in the world, three great lines of stone that no army could break through for a thousand years.

It had a secret weapon too. Greek fire: a liquid flame that burned even on water, sprayed from bronze tubes onto enemy ships. Its recipe was such a close secret that, to this day, no one is quite sure how it was made.
So the empire endured. Emperors came and went. Enemies attacked and were beaten back. The walls held. The gold flowed. For century after century, Byzantium seemed like it might last for ever.

But an empire, like a person, grows old. Slowly, over hundreds of years, Byzantium shrank. Provinces were lost. Rivals grew bolder. By the end, the great city stood almost alone, a glorious head with barely a body left. And a new power was rising in the east.

image.note: Map shrinking to a single dot

chapters.title: The Ottomans and the Fall of the Great City

pages.text: That new power was the Ottomans. They began as a small band of warriors in Anatolia, in what is now Turkey. Within a few generations they had built one of the largest and longest-lasting empires in history.

The Ottomans were brilliant organisers. They gathered many peoples, Turks, Greeks, Arabs, and more, under one ruler, called the sultan, and let each keep their own faith and customs so long as they obeyed and paid their taxes.

Their army was the finest of its age. At its core stood the janissaries, foot soldiers trained from boyhood, loyal only to the sultan, marching to the beat of their own drums. Europe had seen nothing like them.
By the 1400s the Ottomans had spread around Constantinople on every side. The old Roman city was now an island of Byzantium in an Ottoman sea. Everyone could see what must come next.

In 1453 the Ottoman throne passed to a young sultan named Mehmed. He was just twenty-one, and he wanted one thing above all others: the city with the unbreakable walls. People said it could not be taken. Mehmed decided he would take it.
The walls had turned back army after army for a thousand years. Stone three layers deep. A ditch before them. Towers along them. No ladder was long enough, no ram was strong enough.

image.note: Close view of the great walls

pages.text: So Mehmed did not use ladders. He built cannon: the largest guns the world had ever seen, one so vast it took sixty oxen to drag it and could hurl a stone the weight of a grown horse. For the first time, walls that had never fallen began to crack.
For weeks the great guns thundered. The defenders, far too few, patched the broken walls each night by torchlight, knowing more must come at dawn. They were brave. They were also badly outnumbered.

Then Mehmed did something astonishing. Unable to sail his ships past the city's chained harbour, he had them dragged overland, over greased logs, across the hills, and slipped them into the water behind the defences overnight. The defenders woke to find a fleet where no fleet could be.

image.note: Ships hauled over hills on logs

pages.text: On a spring morning in 1453, the walls gave way and the city fell. After more than a thousand years, the Roman empire was finally, truly over. Mehmed rode through the streets of the city he had dreamed of. In time, the great city would take on the name we know it by today: Istanbul.

He did not leave it in ruins. He rebuilt. He filled the empty city with people, mosques, markets, and schools, and made it the capital of his own empire. The great city did not die. It changed hands, and blazed again.

Now travel east, farther than any Ottoman ever marched, to the largest and richest empire on earth in its day: Ming China. While Constantinople was falling, China held perhaps a quarter of all the people alive.

The Ming came to power by driving out foreign rulers and placing a Chinese family back on the throne. Their first emperors were determined that China would be strong, orderly, and never conquered again.

In the capital they built the Forbidden City: a palace so large it was really a city on its own, with walls, moats, and nearly a thousand buildings. Ordinary people could not enter on pain of death. That is how it got its name.
Its halls had golden roofs and blood-red walls, guarded by stone lions and carved dragons. At its centre, upon the Dragon Throne, sat the emperor, whom his people called the Son of Heaven.

To keep out raiders from the north, the Ming rebuilt an old defence into something staggering: the Great Wall of China, thousands of kilometres of stone snaking over the mountains. Most of the wall people visit today was built by the Ming.

But walls alone do not hold an empire together. China was run by officials chosen through the hardest examinations on earth. Any boy, rich or poor, who could pass them might rise to govern a province. Many spent their whole lives studying, and still failed.

Chinese workshops made goods the world hungered for: shining silk, and porcelain so fine and white that in Europe it was simply called "china". These flowed out along the trade roads and filled the empire's treasury.
Then, for a short and dazzling time, China looked outward. The emperor gave a trusted admiral named Zheng He a fleet, and told him to sail out and show the world how great China was.

What a fleet it was. Hundreds of ships. The largest were treasure ships, perhaps five times the length of the little vessels Europeans were then sailing. Zheng He crossed to India, to Arabia, and all the way to the coast of Africa.

image.note: Treasure ship beside a small European ship

pages.text: He brought wonders home. From Africa came a creature no one at court had ever seen: a giraffe, led on a rope up the palace steps, its head higher than the rooftops. The emperor was delighted.

image.note: Giraffe led into the palace court

pages.text: And then, quite suddenly, it stopped. New emperors decided the voyages cost too much and taught China nothing it needed. The great ships were left to rot. China turned its face inward, and shut the door on the sea. It was not defeated. It chose to stop.

Our last empire rose on the far side of the world, in the Americas, in a place none of the others even knew existed. While China counted its millions, an empire was growing that had never heard of China, or Rome, or anywhere across the sea.

image.note: Map of the Americas, empire marked

pages.text: Its people called themselves the Mexica. We call them the Aztecs. According to their own story, their gods told them to build their city where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus, holding a snake. They found that sign on a marshy island in the middle of a lake.

image.note: Eagle on a cactus with a snake

pages.text: On that unlikely island they built one of the most astonishing cities in all of history: Tenochtitlan. Where others chose hills or harbours, the Aztecs built on water, and turned the lake itself into a fortress.

Long stone causeways ran from the island to the shore, wide enough for many people to walk side by side. Wooden bridges along them could be lifted, so that in one moment the whole city could cut itself off from the land.

To feed so many mouths on an island, the Aztecs invented floating gardens called chinampas: rafts of mud and reeds, anchored with willow trees, growing maize, beans, and flowers on the water. A city on a lake grew its own food upon the lake.
Canals ran through the streets like roads made of water, busy with canoes. Visitors from across the sea would later write that they could not believe their eyes, and wondered if they were dreaming.

At the city's heart lay a market so huge that tens of thousands of people came to it every single day. You could buy gold, feathers, chocolate, medicine, sandals, and jaguar skins, all counted out not in coins but in cacao beans.

What held this empire together? A strong army, and tribute: conquered towns sent gold, cloth, and food to the capital. And binding it all, a shared belief in mighty gods, above all Huitzilopochtli, god of the sun, and Tlaloc, who sent the rain.

The Aztecs were remarkable makers and thinkers. They tracked the stars, kept two calendars at once, and engineered a city on water, with clean drinking channels flowing right into it. All this they built without iron, without the wheel for carts, and without any beast to pull a plough.

Picture it one last time: a white city shining on a blue lake, ringed by mountains, its causeways crowded, its temples rising above the water, home to more people than almost any city in Europe. For its age, Tenochtitlan was a wonder of the world.

Four empires. Three continents. Rome's stubborn eastern half, the sweeping Ottomans, the vast and ordered Ming, the shining Aztecs on their lake. They never met. Yet across all that distance, their stories rhyme. Remember our two questions.

What held them together? Look back and you find the same answers again and again. Strong armies. Roads and causeways for soldiers and traders. Trusted money and busy markets. A ruler at the centre. And a shared belief that made strangers feel like one people.

What pulled them apart? Here too the answers rhyme. Byzantium grew old and was overcome by a stronger enemy. The Ottomans stretched so wide they slowly weakened. Ming China turned inward by choice, and closed the door.

And the Aztecs? Their world changed for ever when strangers arrived from across the sea, carrying weapons, and illnesses that the Americas had never known. In a few short years, the shining city on the lake was gone. No empire, however clever, is safe from a world it did not know was coming.
This is the hardest lesson of all. No empire lasts for ever. Not Rome. Not Byzantium with its unbreakable walls. Not the Ming with a quarter of the world. Every single one, in the end, came down.

And yet they are not truly gone. They left their walls and their words behind. They left roads, coins, recipes, calendars, and stories. Istanbul still stands. The Great Wall still climbs the hills. The word "china" is still on your kitchen shelf.

You began this book with the empires of Africa, and you have travelled to three more continents since. Ghana and Mali, Byzantium and the Ottomans, the Ming and the Aztecs: they are not separate stories at all. They are chapters of one long human story, and you are its newest reader.

image.note: World map, all empires lit together

pages.text: Every empire in this book began small: a band of warriors, a family, a marsh, an island. Each one grew, and dazzled, and fell, and left something behind. Somewhere, the next great story is beginning small right now. Where will you go looking for it?

image.note: Child looking out at a wide horizon

pages.text: Timeline. Byzantine Empire: about 330 to 1453. Ottoman Empire: about 1300 to 1922. Ming China: 1368 to 1644. Aztec Empire: about 1345 to 1521.

Words to know. Empire: many peoples under one ruler. Emperor: the ruler of an empire. Siege: surrounding a city to force it to give in. Tribute: goods a conquered people must send their ruler. Causeway: a raised road across water. Official: a person who helps govern.

image.note: A small labelled panel: an emperor's crown, a raised causeway, a bundle of tribute goods, a besieged city wall

pages.text: Four empires down. Hundreds more are waiting: Persia, the Inca, the Mongols who once rode from China to Europe. Every one began small. Every one has a story. Which will you explore next?
